## What it is

146 organizations placed across two lifecycles. The **research lifecycle** runs
from literature grounding through synthesis, peer review, and clinical or
regulatory translation. The **consumer decision lifecycle** picks up where that
stops, and is the reason this release exists: encounter, explore, ground,
evaluate, translate, contextualize, decide, act, observe, revise.

193 sources, each dated and tagged with what kind of evidence it is: a
peer-reviewed paper, an independent party's announcement, a news report, or an
organization describing itself. That last column is the reason to build it. Most
market maps cite company websites and present the result as market intelligence.
Here the source class travels with the claim.

## The finding worth the trouble

Follow the chain to its end and the last stage empties out. Almost nothing is
built to **revise**: to find out the thing is not working, and stop.

That is structural rather than lazy. Stopping needs a rule set in advance. A rule
needs to know whether the thing is working. That needs a benefit signal, and
[we built surveillance for harm and almost none for
benefit](../we-measure-harm-we-mean-benefit/). So nothing tells you it is
working, no stopping rule can be written, and nothing flows back to steer what
gets studied next. Everything clustered near the decision is built to start and
to sustain, because stopping requires a measure nobody has.

## What is still wrong with it

This release is published **uncertified**, and the reason is worth stating on the
first screen rather than in a footnote: the certification harness reads the
previous release's schema, so it parses zero entities from this one and every
entity-level check has silently not run.

The checks that still work found that **87% of sources carry no date** and **88%
are organizations describing themselves** — defensible for what a product claims
to do, not for whether it works.

Three findings stand beyond that: the delta cannot represent a removal, "reviewed
baseline" covers 95 entries nobody reviewed, and one acquisition is blocked rather
than verified. Stage counts remain our coding rather than the companies', so they
describe a vocabulary and should not be quoted as findings.

**[Full release notes, with the certification detail and what was corrected after
publishing →](releases/2026-08-01-r2/)**

Keeping the detail in the release record rather than on this page is deliberate.
A map that accumulates every past defect on its front screen becomes a catalogue
of its own mistakes, and stops being usable for the thing it is for. The record
should be complete; the map should be current.

## How entries get on it

Every stage now has a written inclusion test, and each is written so that it
**excludes something**. A stage whose test excludes nothing is a vocabulary
rather than a classification, and its counts cannot be quoted.

**[Read the tests in full →](method.html)**

They were adopted in August and apply from the September release, so the map
above does not yet reflect them. Where the two disagree, the method page is the
standard and this map is behind it. Applying them cuts the decision layer from
seven organizations to one — a smaller, less impressive, more defensible number,
and the first one on this page that could be quoted.

## What changes each release

Each refresh produces a changelog: who was added, who was removed, who quietly
repositioned, and the one worth watching, whose claim moved from a press release
to an independently verified result.

The map is the artifact. **The changelog is the product.**

**There is no changelog yet.** Both builds so far carry the same date — r2
superseded the August baseline the day it shipped — so there is no month-over-month
pair to diff and none can exist before September. That edition will produce the
first one, and it will be dominated by the taxonomy change rather than by the
market: a *method* diff, not a market one. October is the first honest
like-for-like comparison. Saying so now seems better than letting a monthly
promise accumulate quietly against an empty directory.

## What would make us stop

The essay this map came out of closes by asking what a product would have to
observe to tell you to stop using it. It would be a poor advertisement for that
standard if the map had no answer.

So: **if the November release has not drawn corrections from people who build in
this space, the map drops to quarterly or moves to the archive.** Correction-as-
contribution is the whole premise — that a landscape published with its holes
marked invites people to fill them. If nobody does, the premise is wrong, and the
right response is to stop rather than to keep publishing a monthly artifact
nobody corrects.

That is a real threshold with a date attached, and it is the same test we ask of
everyone else on the map.

## Fix something

Every entry carries a *suggest a correction* link that opens a message naming
that specific organization. If you build in this space and we have described you
wrongly, that is the fastest way to fix it, and corrections get credited in the
following release.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Every build, with its notes and its certification —
[the release archive](releases/).** Releases are immutable once published;
corrections appear as new entries rather than edits.
:::
